nature-econ-792.title: Discounted cash flow: valuing a project by its future payments
nature-econ-792.text: Coal mines in the UK were valued this way as early as 1801. Discounted cash flow analysis values a project, company or security by allowing for the time value of money in the cash it should bring in. Every future cash flow is estimated and discounted, usually at the cost of capital, and the sum is the {{ref:nature-val-014}}. The rate combines the time value of money, captured by the risk-free rate, with a risk premium for the chance the cash flows never arrive. Run in reverse, taking a known price and solving for the rate, the method gives the {{ref:nature-econ-816}} or the yield of a {{ref:nature-mkt-065}}. Irving Fisher first set it out in modern terms in 1930, and John Burr Williams in 1938. It is widely used in finance, real estate, actuarial science and patent valuation. Its forecasts assume the future resembles the past. Small changes to the inputs can swing the result greatly, especially the terminal value, the worth given to everything beyond the forecast. Traditional DCF also counts only financial costs and benefits, leaving out environmental, social and governance performance.

nature-econ-816.title: Internal rate of return: a project's break-even rate
nature-econ-816.text: Suppose a project costs 123,400 up front and then returns 36,200, 54,800 and 48,100 over three years. Its internal rate of return, or IRR, is 5.96%. That is the yearly rate at which the {{ref:nature-val-014}}, or NPV, of all its cash flows equals zero. It is called internal because it ignores outside factors such as the risk-free rate, inflation, the cost of capital or financial risk. Estimated in advance, it predicts a future annual return; measured afterwards, it shows the return actually achieved. A project whose estimated IRR beats the firm's cost of capital for it is profitable. IRR measures a project's profitability or efficiency, while NPV measures how much value it adds. A negative NPV does not necessarily mean a loss. It means the IRR falls below the required rate. For loans and deposits, the IRR is also called the effective interest rate. The modified internal rate of return was developed to fix some of its problems and to rank projects of unequal size.

nature-econ-758.title: The real interest rate: what a loan earns after inflation
nature-econ-758.text: If inflation equals the interest rate on a loan, the lender gains nothing in buying power: the real rate is zero. The real interest rate is the rate after allowing for inflation, while the nominal rate is the rate before that adjustment. Real rates measure what is repaid against the buying power the money had when it was lent. So lenders and borrowers accept a nominal rate made up of the real rate they require plus the inflation they expect. When nominal rates sit below inflation, real rates turn negative. The {{ref:nature-econ-833}} links real rates, nominal rates and the inflation rate. It works with projected rates, called ex ante, or historical ones, called ex post.

nature-econ-806.title: Risk pooling: many pay so that a few are made whole
nature-econ-806.text: An insurer cannot know which customer will suffer a loss. Across a large group, though, predicted losses come close to actual ones, as the law of large numbers shows. That is what makes risk pooling work: gathering money from many insured people or firms to pay the losses that only some of them will suffer. Because policies cover members of large classes, the insurer can rely on that law. Each member is protected for a fee, which depends on how often and how badly the insured event tends to happen. A person or firm can instead self-insure by setting money aside for possible losses. Some communities, including the Amish and some Muslim groups, rely on mutual support from fellow members when disaster strikes rather than on insurance contracts.

nature-econ-779.title: Annuities: equal payments at regular intervals
nature-econ-779.text: A monthly mortgage payment, a pension payment and an insurance premium have something in common. Each is an annuity: a series of equal payments made at regular intervals, usually for a limited term. Life insurers commonly sell annuities. A person pays a lump sum or premiums in return for regular payments, often for retirement. An annuity-immediate pays at the end of each period, like mortgage repayments; an annuity-due pays at the start, like rent. An annuity that continues indefinitely is a {{ref:nature-econ-763}}. Its value is stated as a value today or at a later date, by discounting or accumulating the payments at a stated interest rate. Annuities have a long history. In medieval and early modern Europe they let lenders provide credit where direct interest-bearing loans were restricted. By the 16th and 17th centuries, governments in the Dutch Republic, France and England sold them to raise money.

nature-econ-814.title: What sets the interest rate on a loan
nature-econ-814.text: A loan to a developing country carries a higher interest rate than a loan to the US government. Market interest rates are set in places such as the money market, markets for tradable debt and banks, and each loan's rate reflects several factors. First is opportunity cost: lenders weigh the other uses of their money, including returns elsewhere. Second is inflation. A lender putting off spending wants at least enough to cover rising prices, so the nominal rate is roughly the real rate plus inflation. Third is a risk premium for the chance of default, which is why loans to developing countries cost more. Fourth is time. Shorter loans usually carry less default and inflation risk, so short-term rates often sit below long-term ones, an upward-sloping yield curve. Fifth is ease of resale: lenders want a higher return on something hard to sell quickly at a fair price than on something easy to sell, or liquid. Finally, a {{ref:nature-econ-561}} strongly influences short-term rates, one of its main tools.

nature-econ-774.title: Knightian uncertainty: the risks no one can put odds on
nature-econ-774.text: In 1921 Frank Knight drew a line that economists still use. In his book Risk, Uncertainty, and Profit, he separated measurable risk from uncertainty that cannot be measured or turned into probabilities. That second kind now bears his name. Knight held that measurable uncertainty, risk proper, is so different that it is not really uncertainty at all. Known risks can be insured because they come with a defined set of odds, a probability distribution. True uncertainties lack one and can lead to extreme outcomes. Knight called the people who bear such uncertainty entrepreneurs, so entrepreneurship research studies how uncertainty creates opportunities. The concept admits a basic limit to knowledge and an essential unpredictability of future events. It remains largely informal: there is no single best formal system of probability and belief to represent it.

nature-econ-777.title: Ambiguity aversion: preferring the odds you know
nature-econ-777.text: One urn holds 50 red and 50 black balls. Another holds 100 balls in an unknown mix. Asked to bet, people prefer the first urn. This result, the Ellsberg paradox, first revealed ambiguity aversion: a preference for risks whose odds are known over risks whose odds are unknown. It differs from risk aversion, which compares a gamble with its expected value when the odds are known. Risk aversion is mainly put down to diminishing marginal utility, but ambiguity aversion has no widely accepted main cause. It has been used to explain incomplete contracts, swings in share prices and selective abstention in elections. Greater ambiguity aversion also raises demand for insurance, as people dislike unknown events affecting their lives and property. Experiments suggest attitudes to ambiguity depend on context, so a measure from one setting may not predict behavior in another.

nature-econ-746.title: The discount rate: how fast the future shrinks
nature-econ-746.text: Start-up firms are judged by a tougher yardstick than established companies. The yardstick is the discount rate: the rate at which the charge for delaying a payment must grow as the delay gets longer. Its yearly version, the discount yield, is the share of the original debt that must be paid to delay payment for one year. In financial calculations the rate is usually set equal to the cost of capital. It may be raised to allow for the risk that expected cash flows will not arrive. That is why start-ups typically get higher rates, reflecting disadvantages such as hard-to-sell shares and few willing investors. The starting point is the risk-free rate, the return from risk-free securities such as government debt. The {{ref:nature-econ-845}} builds a discount rate as that risk-free rate plus beta, a measure of how much a share moves with the market, times the equity market risk premium.

nature-econ-752.title: The social discount rate: how much the future counts in public choices
nature-econ-752.text: A highway, a school or a program to protect the environment brings costs and benefits that stretch far ahead. The social discount rate is the discount rate used to value money spent on such public or social projects. It puts a present value on costs and benefits that come later, such as future maintenance or future cuts in pollution. It is critical when costs and benefits are spread unevenly over a long time. The stakes are high. A higher rate makes a social project less likely to be funded, and a small rise in the rate can matter enormously for benefits far in the future. Governments pick very different numbers. The US Office of Management and Budget recommends about 7%, as a pretax return on private capital, while HM Treasury sets 3.5% for the UK public sector. Developed nations typically use lower rates (3–7%) than developing nations (8–15%). At bottom, the rate reflects how a society values welfare today against welfare in the future. Economists have no consensus and no one-size-fits-all rate, given national differences. The choice remains a long-running and fierce debate, sharpened by the {{ref:nature-clim-268}}.

nature-econ-845.title: The capital asset pricing model: rewarding only the risk you cannot escape
nature-econ-845.text: Some risk can be escaped by spreading money across many holdings, and some cannot. The capital asset pricing model, or CAPM, rewards only the second kind. It gives the return a share or other holding should be expected to earn, given how much it moves with the overall market. It uses beta, the holding's sensitivity to market-wide risk that spreading cannot remove, plus the expected market return and the risk-free return. Required return = risk-free rate + beta × market risk premium. A beta of 1.5 means a 10% market rise brings a 15% rise in the share. Treynor, Sharpe, Lintner and Mossin developed the model independently in the 1960s, building on Markowitz, and Sharpe won the 1990 Nobel Prize for it. Its required return serves as the discount rate for a holding's future cash flows, and it is one model used to choose rates in {{ref:nature-val-001}}. Yet the model fails many empirical tests. Fama and French argued in 2004 that this failure makes most of its applications invalid. It stays popular for its simplicity.

nature-econ-838.title: Stochastic dominance: when one gamble beats another for everyone
nature-econ-838.text: An insurance policy with a lower premium and better cover is better whatever happens. That is statewise dominance, the simplest case of stochastic dominance. Stochastic dominance ranks risky options so that one is preferred by every decision maker in a broad class. It works even when their exact utility function is unknown. First-order dominance reaches further. A gamble dominates if, for every amount x, it gives at least as high a chance of getting at least x. Everyone who prefers more to less then chooses it. Second-order dominance roughly means less risk with at least as high an average. All risk-averse expected-utility maximizers prefer the dominant gamble, and only here does risk aversion matter. The ranking is partial: some pairs of gambles cannot be ranked at all. A higher expected value is not enough. In one example, gamble C has a higher mean than A yet does not first-order dominate it. The original version of {{ref:nature-econ-067}} even produced violations of first-order dominance.

nature-econ-754.title: Should a life count less because it comes later?
nature-econ-754.text: At a fixed rate of just 1% a year, Tutankhamun should have valued one day of his own life above all the lives alive today. That strange result sits at the heart of the debate over pure time preference. This is the assumption that an experience, or a life, is intrinsically worth more the sooner it occurs. Economists commonly build it into their models, but most philosophers reject it. The philosopher Toby Ord says most philosophers think it lacks moral justification, and Frank Ramsey called it ethically indefensible. Derek Parfit compared it to an indefensible spatial discount rate that would care less about effects with every yard of distance. Others defend it. Andreas Mogensen argues a positive rate can be justified by kinship, since common-sense morality lets people favor those closer to them. Ordinary attitudes offer a clue. Asked about the welfare of others rather than their own, most people's apparent pure time preference shrinks or vanishes. Yet the opposite extreme has critics too. Weighting future generations fully, they warn, can lead to a 'Pascal's mugging' conclusion that present welfare barely matters. The question remains open.

nature-econ-755.title: Discounting the climate: how one number shapes climate policy
nature-econ-755.text: In 2006 the {{ref:nature-clim-268}} warned that world output risked a 20% cut unless 1% of world output was spent now to reduce global warming. Critics objected that its findings partly rested on an extremely low pure time preference rate of 0.1%. A common misconception holds that Stern used a zero discount rate. In fact its projections used many positive rates while taking time preference near zero. The choice of rate for the benefits of cutting emissions of heat-trapping gases is one of the most controversial questions in climate economics. Rates used in climate studies of costs and benefits range from zero to over 3%. The rate is usually positive because resources invested today can, on average, become more resources later. Its size matters enormously. Too high a rate means too little action to cut emissions; too low a rate means too much. A rival model, with a 3% rate declining to 1% over 300 years, found taxes on carbon necessary but much smaller than Stern recommended. US policy has swung as well. Under Obama, the official estimate of damage per ton of carbon emitted was $51/ton at a 3% discount rate; Biden proposed over $190/ton using lower rates. Some argue that giving future generations less weight is ethically indefensible. Others reply that equal weighting yields nonsensical results.

nature-econ-834.title: Real options: the value of waiting and changing course
nature-econ-834.text: Standard {{ref:nature-val-014}} treats managers as passive once money is committed, ignoring their freedom to react as markets turn out. Real options valuation fixes that. It applies the methods used to price financial options, contracts giving a right to buy or sell, to decisions about real projects. A real option is the right, but not the duty, to defer, abandon, expand, stage or shrink a project. In one worked example, NPV says invest now for a gain of 1M, but waiting a year for information is worth 1.21M, so the firm should wait. A negative NPV need not rule out acting either. Opening one store and expanding later if demand is high can be worth 0.41M. A mining firm can likewise delay work on a deposit until markets turn favorable. Real options are most valuable when uncertainty is high and managers have room and willingness to change course. Stewart Myers of MIT coined the term 'real option' in 1977, after the Black–Scholes work of 1973 made financial options analyzable.

nature-econ-802.title: Climateflation: when a warming climate raises prices
nature-econ-802.text: Heat, droughts and floods hit farm output, and shoppers feel it at the checkout. Climateflation is inflation driven by {{ref:nature-hist-007}}, through its effects on food production and supply chains. Isabel Schnabel of the European Central Bank first used the term. In 2022–2023, climate-driven heat in Europe raised food prices by about 0.7%, adding about 0.3% to overall inflation. The same study found that warming expected by 2035 could raise these effects by 30–50%. A related term, fossilflation, describes inflation caused by fossil fuel prices, which push up transport, food and shipping costs.

nature-econ-803.title: Inflation targeting: steering prices toward a set goal
nature-econ-803.text: In 1990 New Zealand became the first country to adopt an official inflation target. Inflation targeting is a policy in which the {{ref:nature-econ-561}} keeps adjusting its interest rate to steer inflation toward that target. It has since spread to most developed countries, and in most OECD countries the target is about 2%. Why not aim for zero? Research suggests true inflation runs about one percentage point below the official figure. A 2% target keeps true inflation from nearing zero or tipping into deflation, a fall in prices.

nature-econ-804.title: What causes inflation: a centuries-old argument
nature-econ-804.text: Rival schools have disputed the causes of inflation for centuries, from the quantity theory of money against the real bills doctrine to Keynesians against monetarists. In 1936 Keynes argued that wages and prices are sticky in the short run but respond gradually to swings in demand. In the 1960s Milton Friedman's {{ref:nature-econ-547}} challenged this view, holding that inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon. In the 1970s the link between inflation and joblessness broke down, which was eventually put down to changing expectations. Since about 2000, the common view gives roles to demand shocks, supply shocks and inflation expectations.

nature-econ-835.title: Risk neutrality: caring only about the average
nature-econ-835.text: A risk-neutral investor would put every dollar into the single holding with the highest expected yield. A risk-averse one spreads money around. Risk-neutral preferences are neither risk averse nor risk seeking: the person cares only about the expected payoff, not how uncertain it is. The utility function is a straight line in money, so maximizing expected utility is the same as maximizing expected money. Risk averters have concave utility, and risk lovers convex. The QALY model in health economics, which counts quality-adjusted years of life, assumes risk-neutral behavior, among other things.

nature-econ-791.title: The discount function: weighting rewards across time
nature-econ-791.text: How much is a reward next year worth next to one today? A discount function answers by giving the weights an economic model places on rewards received at different times. Often each period's enjoyment is assumed to count on its own, called time-separable utility. Total utility from a stream of things consumed over time is then the sum of each period's utility, weighted by the discount function. The two most common examples are {{ref:nature-econ-794}} and {{ref:nature-econ-748}}.

nature-econ-794.title: Exponential discounting: the same shrinkage every period
nature-econ-794.text: In finance, discounting is normally modeled as exponential. Exponential discounting is a discount function in which value falls by the same proportion for each extra unit of delay. Total utility is the sum of each period's utility multiplied by a fixed weight, δ, raised to the power of the time period. So the trade-off between consuming at two dates depends only on how far apart they are. That makes it dynamically consistent: preferences do not change as time passes unless new information arrives. It is the most common assumption in economics because of its simplicity. Yet alternatives such as {{ref:nature-econ-748}} have more empirical support.

nature-econ-748.title: Hyperbolic discounting: why tomorrow's self disagrees with today's
nature-econ-748.text: Many people take $50 now over $100 in a year. Yet almost everyone picks $100 in six years over $50 in five years, though the trade-off is the same. Hyperbolic discounting explains the flip. It is a model of how people devalue delayed rewards in which their choices are not consistent over time. Value falls quickly over short early delays but more slowly over longer ones. In an early study, people were indifferent between $15 now and $30 in 3 months, $60 in 1 year or $100 in 3 years. The implied yearly discount rates fell from 277% to 139% to 63%. The hyperbolic formula is g(D) = 1/(1 + kD), where D is the delay and k sets how strongly rewards are discounted. Its key consequence is temporary preferences for smaller, sooner rewards over larger, later ones, so people make choices their future selves regret. Such reversals were first found in rats and pigeons, so they do not depend on human culture. It is a cornerstone of {{ref:nature-econ-021}}, used to study retirement planning, credit-card borrowing, addiction and procrastination.

nature-econ-775.title: Radical uncertainty: what no research can resolve
nature-econ-775.text: Some uncertainty would yield to enough research. Radical uncertainty would not: it is uncertainty that no available means of gaining knowledge could resolve. John Kay and Mervyn King popularized the term in a book published in March 2020. That is the line between it and Knightian uncertainty. If research could remove the uncertainty, it is not radical.

nature-econ-776.title: Uncertainty in science: what scientists mean and what the public hears
nature-econ-776.text: Scientists and the public often hear the word uncertainty in very different ways. The public can misread scientific uncertainty as ignorance or a lack of consensus. Differences between studies caused by their methods can look like disagreement where agreement actually exists. That gap can be exploited. Deniers of {{ref:nature-hist-007}} followed Frank Luntz's advice to frame global warming as a matter of scientific uncertainty. Scientific uncertainty may also be managed deliberately to reach certain goals.

nature-econ-759.title: How central banks use interest rates
nature-econ-759.text: From 1954 to 2008, the US federal funds rate, the key US policy rate, varied between about 0.25% and 19%. Each {{ref:nature-econ-561}} sets target interest rates as a main tool for influencing spending, inflation and joblessness. They usually cut rates when they want more spending by firms and households. Very low rates carry risks, feeding bubbles in property and share markets. At the extreme, a zero interest-rate policy sets the target near zero. There conventional policy struggles, because market rates are hard to push below zero.

nature-econ-761.title: Liquidity preference: the pull of ready cash
nature-econ-761.text: Cash can be spent at once, while some holdings take time and money to turn back into cash. Liquidity preference is the tendency of people and firms to prefer holding cash, or holdings that are easily sold, over ones that are harder to convert. It shows up as a gap in yields between holdings with different maturities and conversion costs. It also explains why longer-lasting holdings usually have to offer higher yields.

nature-econ-760.title: Negative interest rates: paying to lend
nature-econ-760.text: In theory, no lender should accept less than 0%, since simply holding cash avoids a guaranteed loss. Yet the European Central Bank from 2014 and the Bank of Japan from early 2016 used negative rates, alongside {{ref:nature-econ-564}}. A negative interest rate charges savers for holding money and has been described as a tax on holding money. Silvio Gesell proposed the idea in the late 19th century. During the European debt crisis, some countries' government debt sold at negative yields, so lenders in effect paid governments to borrow.
